lead: A hypothesis test asks whether sample data are consistent with a stated model. You assume a null hypothesis H0, choose an alternative H1 that carries the claim you want to support, and measure the distance between the data and H0 with a test statistic. Because samples vary, a decision rule can raise a false alarm. The test fixes, before sampling, a small probability α for that false alarm. This logic is used in quality control, A/B tests on apps, clinical trials and checking whether a UPI payment failure rate has changed.
prereq: You need Unit 2 (probability) and Unit 5 (sampling distributions and standard error); the test statistics in this unit are built in Chapter 6.2 onward.

sections.h3: Hypotheses, test statistic and rejection region

blocks.text: The null hypothesis H<sub>0</sub> is the claim assumed true while the test runs. It usually states no change or no effect, such as H<sub>0</sub>: μ = 1000 h for the mean battery life μ. The alternative hypothesis H<sub>1</sub> is the claim you want evidence for. It can be one-sided with H<sub>1</sub>: μ < 1000 h or H<sub>1</sub>: μ > 1000 h, or two-sided with H<sub>1</sub>: μ ≠ 1000 h. H<sub>0</sub> always contains the equality used to compute the null distribution. H<sub>1</sub> decides the direction of the evidence.

blocks.where: T is the test statistic; estimate is the sample quantity; null value is the value in H<sub>0</sub>; standard error is the standard deviation of the estimate.

blocks.text: A test statistic T is a number computed from the sample whose distribution is known when H0 is true. Large |T| means the sample is far from H0. The critical region, also called the rejection region, is the set of T values that lead to rejecting H0. Its boundary is chosen from α. For a mean with known σ, T = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n); x̄ is the sample mean, μ0 the null mean, σ the population standard deviation and n the sample size. Chapters 6.2 to 6.5 give the standard statistics.

sections.h3: Type I error, type II error and power

blocks.text: The level of significance α is the maximum probability of rejecting H<sub>0</sub> when H<sub>0</sub> is true. It is fixed before the sample is taken. A type I error is rejecting a true H<sub>0</sub>; its probability is α. A type II error is failing to reject a false H<sub>0</sub>; its probability is β. Power is 1 − β, the probability of rejecting H<sub>0</sub> when H<sub>0</sub> is false. A test with high power detects a real departure from H<sub>0</sub> more often.

Some syllabi call α the size of the test and call the rejection region the critical region. For fixed sample size, lowering α makes a type I error less likely but usually raises β. Taking a larger sample can lower both errors. “Fail to reject H<sub>0</sub>” is not the same as “H<sub>0</sub> is true”; the data may simply be too weak to show a difference.

sections.h3: p-value, decision rule and confidence intervals

blocks.text: The p-value is the smallest α at which the observed statistic would reject H<sub>0</sub>. It is computed after the sample. For a one-sided test, it is the probability, under H<sub>0</sub>, of a statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the observed one in the direction of H<sub>1</sub>. For a two-sided test with a symmetric null distribution, double the one-tailed area. In the battery example, z = −2.1 gives one-tailed p = P(Z ≤ −2.1) = 0.0179.

Decision rule: reject H<sub>0</sub> if p ≤ α, or equivalently if T lies in the critical region. Otherwise fail to reject H<sub>0</sub>. The p-value is not the probability that H<sub>0</sub> is true. It is a probability of the data, computed assuming H<sub>0</sub>. A small p says the data are unlikely under H<sub>0</sub>, not that H<sub>0</sub> has a small probability.

Confidence intervals give the same decision for two-sided tests. A two-sided test of H<sub>0</sub>: μ = μ<sub>0</sub> at level α rejects H<sub>0</sub> exactly when μ<sub>0</sub> lies outside the 100(1 − α)% confidence interval for μ. Unit 5 gives interval estimation. For one-sided tests the match is with a one-sided bound.

figure.caption: The test fixes α before the sample, then compares the computed p-value with α; the worked example gives p = 0.0179 and α = 0.05, so the decision is reject H0.

spec.title: Six steps of a test
spec.aria: A vertical flowchart from stating hypotheses to fixing alpha, sampling, computing a statistic, finding a p-value, and deciding.

examples.question: A battery maker claims a mean life of 1000 h. Test H0: μ = 1000 h against H1: μ < 1000 h at α = 0.05. A sample gives test statistic z = −2.1. Find the p-value and decide. Use the standard normal table.
steps: State the hypotheses: H0: μ = 1000 h and H1: μ < 1000 h. The alternative is lower-tailed because it says less than 1000 h.
The significance level is already fixed: α = 0.05.
The observed test statistic is z = −2.1. It has no units.
The p-value is the lower-tail probability: p = P(Z ≤ −2.1). From the standard normal table, Φ(−2.1) = 0.0179.
Decision: reject H0. The sample supports the claim that the mean battery life is less than 1000 h.
examples.answer: Reject H0; the sample supports the claim that mean battery life is less than 1000 h.
examples.check:
from statistics import NormalDist
z = -2.1
alpha = 0.05
p = NormalDist().cdf(z)
print(z)
print(round(p, 4))
print(alpha)

code.code:
from statistics import NormalDist
z = -2.1
alpha = 0.05
p = NormalDist().cdf(z)
print(z)
print(round(p, 4))
print(alpha)

traps: The p-value is not P(H<sub>0</sub> true). It is P(data as extreme or more extreme | H<sub>0</sub>).
α is chosen before the sample. Changing α after seeing p is data snooping.
One-sided and two-sided p-values differ. For a symmetric two-sided test, p = 2 × one-tailed area; do not double a one-sided p unless the test is two-sided.
Type I and type II errors are not interchangeable: type I rejects a true H<sub>0</sub>; type II fails to reject a false H<sub>0</sub>. Power = 1 − β, not α.
“Fail to reject H<sub>0</sub>” does not prove H<sub>0</sub>. A small sample may have low power and miss a real effect.

quiz.q: Define H0 and H1 in a test of a population mean.
quiz.a: H0 is the null hypothesis, the claim assumed true and containing equality, such as μ = μ0. H1 is the alternative hypothesis, the claim you want evidence for, such as μ < μ0, μ > μ0 or μ ≠ μ0.

quiz.q: What is a type I error? What is its probability?
quiz.a: A type I error is rejecting H0 when H0 is true. Its probability is the significance level α.

quiz.q: Why do we say “fail to reject H0” rather than “accept H0”?
quiz.a: Failure to reject means the sample does not give strong enough evidence against H0. It does not prove H0 true; a type II error may have occurred, especially when power is low.

quiz.q: A one-sided test has p = 0.03 and α = 0.05. Decide. If the same statistic were used in a two-sided test with p = 0.06, decide at α = 0.05.
quiz.a: One-sided: 0.03 ≤ 0.05, so reject H0. Two-sided: 0.06 > 0.05, so fail to reject H0.

quiz.q: A two-sided z-test gives z = 2.1. Use Φ(2.1) = 0.9821 to find the p-value and decide at α = 0.05.
quiz.a: Upper-tail area = 1 − 0.9821 = 0.0179. Two-sided p = 2 × 0.0179 = 0.0358. Since 0.0358 ≤ 0.05, reject H0.

quiz.q: A test at α = 0.01 fails to reject H0. Can you conclude H0 is true? Explain using β and power.
quiz.a: No. The data may be consistent with H0 because the test has low power or the sample is small. A type II error has probability β; power is 1 − β. Failure to reject is not proof of H0.

quiz.q: Why is a p-value not the probability that H0 is true? Use the battery example with p = 0.0179.
quiz.a: The p-value is computed assuming H0 is true. It is P(Z ≤ −2.1 | H0) = 0.0179, a probability about the data. P(H0 true) needs prior information and is not given by this calculation.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, A/B tests run many comparisons at once, so teams control the false discovery rate rather than a single α. Sequential tests let analysts peek at data without inflating type I error. Bayesian hypothesis tests replace α and p-values with posterior probabilities and Bayes factors. Search for “false discovery rate”, “sequential testing” and “Bayes factor”.
